paras: The attempted lynching of Lee McElroy was a mob's attempt in Louisville, Kentucky, in April 1888 to lynch a 15-year-old Black youth accused of carrying off a young white child to hold for ransom. Police held off the crowd, and McElroy was taken to jail alive. A Louisville wire story carried the case to papers from New York and Washington to Utah, Kansas and Wyoming, most of them saying that only his youth had kept him from being lynched.

According to the Louisville wire dated April 13, McElroy, described as "a colored youth, 15 years of age," took a three-year-old child from a front yard that morning. Most versions named the father as Robert Hoskins, "a well-known business man," while the Wheeling Register called him "a wealthy citizen."

A search followed, and the youth was found hiding with the child "in the corner of a lot near his home." He was reported to have said that he meant to hold the child for ransom, and one headline read "He Admits the Act and Did It to Get Money."

A separate Louisville dispatch dated April 16 gave a fuller and partly different account, in which the youth seized the child in his arms and ran down Broadway toward the commons before he was found "crouching in a fence corner out in the country." In that version he gave his name as Levi McElroy and said he "meant to do it no harm." The wire said the neighborhood was "greatly excited" and that he would have been lynched but for his "extreme youth."

The April 16 dispatch instead reported that "an effort was made to lynch the negro" and that officers drew their revolvers and kept the crowd back, and a Maysville, Kentucky, brief likewise said police "barely saved the child-stealer from being lynched."

McElroy was held in jail. According to an added paragraph in the Wichita Eagle, the child's father went to the jail that night and asked to see him, but was refused because officials feared he might kill the youth. No report of a charge, hearing, trial or sentence was found in the coverage.

Nearly all coverage came from one Louisville wire story of April 13, printed the next day by The Sun of New York, the National Republican in Washington and The Salt Lake Herald, and by the Springfield Daily Republic in Ohio the same day. The story kept running in shorter form for a week, in the Wichita Eagle on April 15, the Helena Weekly Herald and the Fremont Clipper of Wyoming on April 19, and The Cambria Freeman in Pennsylvania on April 20.

Headlines dwelt on the youth and his race, from "A Child Stolen by a Colored Youth" in The Sun and "Kidnaped by a Negro Boy" in the Dakotaian to "A Bold, Bad Black" in The Salt Lake Herald. The wire marked the child as "white" and called the youth "the negro boy," and no paper questioned the accusation or criticized the crowd. Instead, most papers treated the lynching as something that would have happened but for the boy's age, and the Fremont Clipper put it as "His age saved him from a lynching." The Springfield paper, under the headline "Attempted Abduction," left out the lynching sentence altogether.

The papers differed on details: the child was three years old in the main wire, two in the Maysville brief and an eight-year-old daughter in the April 16 dispatch. The father appeared as Robert Hoskins, R. H. Hopkins, B. H. Hoskins and Robert Haskins, and the Springfield version gave the name Robert Hoskins to the child. The youth was Lee McElroy in the wire but gave the name Levi McElroy in the April 16 dispatch, which is also the only account to say he was found out in the country rather than near his home.
Accounts also differed on why he was not lynched: the wire credited his youth, while the April 16 dispatch and the Maysville brief credited the officers.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of Lee McElroy
bases: A crowd tried to lynch a Black youth accused of kidnapping a white child and was held off by officers (A8, A7); the wire said he would have been lynched but for his youth (A3, A4).

McElroy was not killed: officers kept the crowd at bay (A8) and he was jailed (A6); the papers describe an attempted or threatened lynching by an excited neighborhood crowd of unstated size over an accused kidnapping (A3, A8).
The April 13 Louisville wire (A1, A3, A4) and a separate April 16 Louisville dispatch (A8) agree on the kidnapping accusation, the capture and the near-lynching, though they differ on names and ages.

accounts.label: Louisville wire, April 13
accounts.gist: McElroy, 15, stole the three-year-old Hoskins child for ransom, was found hiding near his home, and would have been lynched by the excited neighborhood but for his youth.

accounts.label: Louisville dispatch, April 16
accounts.gist: A negro youth seized the 8-year-old daughter of B. H. Hoskins and ran toward the commons; found in a fence corner in the country; officers with drawn revolvers held off a lynching attempt.

accounts.label: Maysville brief
accounts.gist: Police caught the youth and the two-year-old child and barely saved him from being lynched.

framing.detail: Most papers ran the April 13 wire nearly verbatim, ending 'but for the extreme youth of the offender he would have been lynched.'
Headlines stressed race and guilt ('A Bold, Bad Black', 'He Admits the Act and Did It to Get Money') while the text reported the near-lynching without criticism of the crowd.
The Springfield version, 'Attempted Abduction', omitted the lynching sentence.

conflicts.note: Same youth; one name in the wire, another in the April 16 dispatch.
The wire's three years is the most widely printed; no account settles it.
A1 gives 'Robert Hoskins' as the child's own name.
